<reason>Both sides were excellent, well-grounded, and format-compliant (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 handling throughout). A's rebuttals were surgically sharp — "custody is not curation," "you cannot campaign on a commons and govern with a locked door," and the "obligation by direction" analysis were genuinely damaging, and A's clipped opening was only a minor cost. But B held the motion's central clause: A conceded that the records which matter most will never sell, and answered B's core pressure (who funds the unsellable ledger?) only with discretionary public grants — public money without a duty. B's closing converted that concession decisively: A ended up endorsing the funding half of the motion and disputing only custody ("concedes the money, quibbles over letterhead" was a fair hit, not mere rhetoric). Meanwhile B's comparative move on capture — "capture by neglect," one official reading beats no usable copy, and nothing in markets compels scanning the boarding-school death list either — neutralized A's strongest line by showing A's compulsion critique applied symmetrically or worse to A's own grant model. A's rebuttal craft was arguably better speech-by-speech, but B made the debate easier to decide on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was B's Pressure Question 1 (who funds the record that never becomes a product?) → A's Rebuttal 2 answer (targeted grants to mission-driven custodians) → B's closing reframe (grants without a duty are leftover charity; CON has conceded the money and only contests custody). That sequence collapsed A's "many keys" alternative into the motion's funding logic. Runner-up: B's Rebuttal 1 turning the consent argument — "A paywall is not confidentiality; it is privacy for those who can pay and exposure for those who cannot" — which flipped A's strongest opening plank.</best_rebuttal>
